answer: GTK4's built-in TextView undo (Ctrl+Z/Ctrl+Y, enabled via the buffer's default enable-undo=True) replays edits through an internal history mechanism that doesn't always route through the same code path that flips GtkTextBuffer's modified flag, so "modified-changed" can fail to fire after undo even though the buffer content actually changed. Don't rely on "modified-changed" alone to track dirty state around undo/redo. Instead, connect to the buffer's "changed" signal (which fires on every content mutation, including undo/redo) and manage your own dirty flag there, e.g. compare against a saved baseline text/hash, or explicitly call buffer.set_modified(True) inside the "changed" handler if it isn't already true. Also confirm you're on a recent GTK4 point release, since undo/modified-tracking interactions have had fixes across 4.x versions. You can also watch buffer.get_can_undo()/get_can_redo() transitions as a supplementary signal around undo actions.

This is a known Tk/Aqua redraw bug on older macOS Tk builds: grid_remove() followed by grid() changes geometry but Tk fails to invalidate the drawing region until some other event (focus, Enter/Leave, click) forces a repaint. The robust fix is to stop using grid_remove()/grid() for page switching and instead keep all page frames gridded into the same cell permanently, switching visibility with tkraise(): place each page once with frame.grid(row=0, column=0, sticky='nsew'), then call frame.tkraise() to switch pages. Since the frame never leaves the geometry manager, there's no remove/re-add redraw path to trigger the bug. If you must keep grid_remove()/grid(), try forcing a redraw afterward with widget.update_idletasks(), root.update(), or a dummy event_generate('<Configure>'), and consider testing with a newer Tcl/Tk (8.6.x) build rather than whatever ships with the old system Python, since this class of repaint bug was fixed in later Tk releases.

That message is transformers' lazy-import wrapper hiding the real exception: "pipeline" itself imports fine, but something it depends on for this task/model failed to import, and the generic LazyModule error masks the actual traceback. Get the real error by importing directly: from transformers.pipelines import pipeline in a fresh cell, or set TRANSFORMERS_VERBOSITY=debug / run in a plain terminal to see the full stack above the final line. Common causes: missing optional deps for this specific model (try pip install accelerate sentencepiece protobuf tiktoken), a torch build mismatch (on Apple Silicon make sure you have the arm64 wheel, not an x86 one under Rosetta - check python -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.backends.mps.is_available())"), or the Jupyter kernel pointing at a different Python/env than the one you installed packages into (check sys.executable vs. where pip installed). Reinstalling torch/transformers rarely fixes this if it's actually a missing optional dependency for that particular model's pipeline class.

With CUDA tensors through torch.multiprocessing.Queue, put() only sends the CUDA IPC handle (metadata) - actual GPU memory isn't copied synchronously, so a naive time.perf_counter_ns() wrapped around put/get mostly measures Python pickling plus pipe/IPC-handle transfer time, not real data-transfer latency, and CUDA calls are asynchronous by default so timings can be misleading unless you synchronize at the right points. You already call torch.cuda.synchronize() on the producer before starting the timer, which is correct; you should also call torch.cuda.synchronize() on the consumer right after queue.get() before stamping ts_end, since reconstructing the tensor from the IPC handle doesn't guarantee the data is complete without a sync. For more accurate GPU-side latency, prefer torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True) recorded at send/receive and read via elapsed_time(), rather than wall-clock perf_counter, since that isolates device-side timing from OS scheduling/serialization noise in the Queue itself.

list.eval can't fan one element out into several (it's strictly element-to-element), so replacing "55" with two values requires exploding the list, doing the replacement row-wise, then re-aggregating back into a list per original row:

mapping = {"55": ["55.11", "55.12"]}
out = (
    df.with_row_index("_idx")
      .explode("a")
      .with_columns(
          pl.col("a").map_elements(lambda x: mapping.get(x, [x]), return_dtype=pl.List(pl.Utf8))
      )
      .explode("a")
      .group_by("_idx", maintain_order=True)
      .agg(pl.col("a"))
      .drop("_idx")
)

This preserves row order and correctly expands "55" into ["55.11","55.12"] wherever it appears, leaving other elements untouched. For large data, a pure-expression version avoiding the Python map_elements callback would be faster (pl.when/then plus a second explode), but explode -> transform -> explode -> group_by is the general idiom for any 1-to-many replacement inside a List column in Polars.

The problem is that regex_values is far too aggressive for a whole-row cleanup: cols = re.sub('\w*\d\w*', '', cols) strips out any token containing a digit, which is exactly what destroys your Date and Number columns, and NLTK's English stopword list actually includes the word "no", so your stopword filter removes it too. The fix isn't a better regex, it's scoping the cleaning to the right column: only run regex_values on the free-text Name column, and leave Date and Number completely untouched - df['Name'] = df['Name'].apply(regex_values). For Status, don't stopword-filter at all - just df['Status'] = df['Status'].str.lower() - or if you reuse the same function, remove "no" (and "yes") from the stopword set first with stopword.discard('no'). Applying one generic "clean everything" function to structured columns like dates/IDs/status flags is the root mistake; treat each column according to what it actually contains instead of running every column through NLP-style text cleaning.

static_argnames=['n', 'omega'] on hamiltonian requires omega to be a concrete, hashable Python value at trace time. That's fine when you call solve_diff directly, but grad(solve_diff, argnums=(1,2,3)) differentiates with respect to omega, so JAX passes a JVPTracer for omega into solve_diff, which forwards it into hamiltonian - where it hits the static-argument machinery and fails to hash. An argument can't simultaneously be "static" (a fixed Python value known at trace time) and "differentiated" (traced). Fix: drop 'omega' from static_argnames on hamiltonian (and on solve_diff if you differentiate w.r.t. it there too), keeping only 'n' static, since n is a genuine shape/structural parameter that's never differentiated. omega should just be a normal traced float argument; jit handles that fine, it will simply retrace when omega's abstract shape/dtype changes, not on every value.

Reindex's failures array only reports bulk-indexing failures, not ingest-pipeline processor failures - if the inference processor has (or defaults to) ignore_failure: true, or a preceding processor swallows errors via on_failure, documents can silently skip embedding generation while the reindex task still reports full success. Check the pipeline definition for ignore_failure/on_failure on the inference processors, and check _nodes/stats/ingest/pipelines plus the ELSER trained model stats (GET _ml/trained_models/.elser_model_2_linux-x86_64/_stats) for inference errors, queue timeouts, or rejected requests - ELSER deployments have limited allocations/threads, and under bulk load some inference calls can time out or get throttled rather than erroring loudly. Also check whether the affected documents actually have non-empty content/name source fields, since a missing/empty input field is commonly skipped without an error. Try _ingest/pipeline/elser_double_embedding_pipeline/_simulate against a few docs missing embeddings, and consider increasing model number_of_allocations/threads and re-running with slower throughput.

This looks like Dynaconf's environment-layer merge logic colliding with @get-resolved lists: when an @get token resolves to a list (calendar_ids) at a path nested underneath tables built up across [default]/[nonprod]/[prod] layers, Dynaconf's dict-merge machinery can treat the list as something to merge key-by-key against whatever structure already exists there, turning it into an index-keyed dict ({'0': 'a', '1': 'b'}) instead of leaving it as a plain list. This is a known rough edge in how Dynaconf merges Box/list structures across environments combined with lazily-resolved @get tokens, not something wrong in your TOML syntax - your carrot branch, which reads "@get google" as one top-level get rather than assembling nested tables plus per-field @gets, avoids it. Workaround: resolve the whole sub-object with one @get (like carrot does) rather than rebuilding the same shape field-by-field with nested tables, or check the latest Dynaconf issue tracker, since list-vs-dict merge handling is a recurring bug area there.

lib_resume_builder_AIHawk isn't a generic PyPI utility - it's a submodule of the AIHawk / Auto_Jobs_Applier_AIHawk job-application project, normally installed as part of that project's own requirements.txt inside a dedicated virtual environment, not as a standalone package you pip install in isolation (that name may not resolve to a working package on PyPI, or may install into the wrong environment). Clone the project repo, create/activate its virtualenv (check the required Python version, historically 3.10), and run pip install -r requirements.txt from the project root so all its pinned dependencies install together. Then verify the interpreter actually running your script is the same one you installed into: python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)" and pip show lib_resume_builder_AIHawk. If you're running this from an IDE or Jupyter, make sure its kernel is pointed at that same virtualenv, since a mismatched interpreter is the most common cause of "installed but still ModuleNotFoundError".

overrideredirect(True) removes window-manager decoration entirely, including the taskbar association, which is why you lose the taskbar icon. On Windows, strip just the caption/title bar while keeping the resizable border and taskbar icon by editing the native window style with ctypes after creation:

import ctypes
GWL_STYLE = -16
WS_CAPTION = 0x00C00000
hwnd = ctypes.windll.user32.GetParent(root.winfo_id())
style = ctypes.windll.user32.GetWindowLongPtrW(hwnd, GWL_STYLE)
ctypes.windll.user32.SetWindowLongPtrW(hwnd, GWL_STYLE, style & ~WS_CAPTION)
root.geometry(root.geometry())

This keeps WS_THICKFRAME (resizable border/drag) and the taskbar's WS_EX_APPWINDOW association intact, since only the caption bit is cleared rather than replacing the whole style like overrideredirect does. You'll need to implement your own drag-to-move (bind mouse events on a custom top strip), since removing the caption also removes native window dragging. This is Windows-specific - there's no single cross-platform tkinter API for partial decoration removal; each OS would need its own native-call approach.

This matches a known class of taskiq-redis issues around RedisScheduleSource-backed dynamic schedules: the consumer group ("taskiq") on the underlying Redis Stream can disappear out from under the worker - e.g. if the stream key gets trimmed/expired/evicted (check maxmemory-policy; anything in the allkeys-* family can evict active taskiq keys under memory pressure) or if the schedule source recreates the stream key without re-running XGROUP CREATE ... MKSTREAM, while your static decorator-based schedules never touch that dynamic path so don't trigger it. Check: (1) redis-cli CONFIG GET maxmemory-policy and set it to noeviction or a volatile-* policy so taskiq's keys aren't evicted; (2) whether anything else (TTL, FLUSHALL, a Redis restart/failover) could remove the stream during the 30-40 minute window; (3) your taskiq-redis version against its GitHub issues for NOGROUP/consumer-group bugs with dynamic schedules - this is a recognized rough edge there, not something obviously wrong in the broker.py shown.

Intermittent ~60s stalls with Gunicorn sync workers usually mean a request got queued behind a thread/worker blocked on something synchronous - a slow or hanging outbound call (DB, API, file I/O) without a timeout, or lock contention on a shared global object (a requests.Session, DB connection, cache, matplotlib state) that isn't actually thread-safe across your 4 threads. Since it's occasional rather than constant, also check whether Gunicorn's worker --timeout (default 30s) is killing and respawning a worker mid-request, which can look like a ~60s hang to the browser (kill + retry). To isolate it: add timestamped logging at the start/end of each callback and around outbound calls, watch Gunicorn's logs for worker timeout/restart lines during a slow reload, and check whether the stall correlates with a specific callback (e.g. a network/DB fetch without an explicit timeout). If it's lock contention, moving to gthread with more workers (fewer threads each) or isolating the shared resource behind a proper connection pool usually resolves it.

A list comprehension is the idiomatic replacement for that loop:

[key for key in d if key[0] == n]

That's already about as pythonic as it gets for a one-off filter - Python doesn't have a built-in dict-key-query mini-language beyond comprehensions/filter(). If you need to query by first element repeatedly for many different n values, it's more efficient to build an index once rather than rescanning the whole dict each time:

from collections import defaultdict
index = defaultdict(list)
for key in d:
    index[key[0]].append(key)

then index[n] is an O(1) lookup. For a single ad-hoc query, just use the comprehension - writing matching_keys as "return [key for key in d if key[0] == n]" is fine and arguably clearer than the explicit accumulator loop, since it says directly "give me the keys matching this predicate" rather than describing the mechanics of building the result list.

This is a real gap in the current typing system, not something you're doing wrong: type[T] only binds T when the argument is an actual class object, but unions, Annotated[...], and other special forms aren't instances of type - they're separate special-form objects - so type checkers can't infer T through them via a plain type[T] parameter. There's no stable, checker-portable annotation today for "a type expression that may be a class, union, or Annotated form, and bind T to what it denotes." There's an active typing-spec proposal (discussed as TypeForm/TypeExpr, roughly PEP 747) to add exactly this kind of annotation, but checker support is limited/experimental as of now, so you can't rely on it broadly yet. Practically: keep your overloads for type[T], accept that unions/Annotated inputs won't infer T precisely in pyright/mypy today, and use cast() at the call sites needing the special-form cases, or track that proposal's adoption if you need this to type-check cleanly long-term.

507 here is very unlikely to be a literal "server out of disk space" - it's far more common for anti-bot/WAF layers (or an overloaded origin behind a CDN) to return unusual 5xx codes as a soft block signal once they detect scraping/rotating-proxy traffic. First confirm what's actually in the 507 response body/headers (fetch it in a browser or curl through the same proxy) rather than assuming genuine capacity exhaustion. Then: add 507 to RETRY_HTTP_CODES (it isn't retried by default) alongside RETRY_ENABLED; slow down and randomize timing with AUTOTHROTTLE_ENABLED=True and a lower CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN; rotate User-Agent together with your proxies, not just IP, since blocking is often keyed on the combination; and check whether your rotating-proxy pool is low-quality/shared/already-blacklisted, which is the most common real cause of a scraper getting blocked intermittently even though manual/browser requests succeed. If none of that helps, the site is likely fingerprinting beyond IP+UA and you may need a headless-browser approach instead of raw Scrapy requests.

MaxNLocator picks its own "nice round number" tick positions within your data range - it doesn't know you want the first tick to be exactly 2, it just fits roughly N evenly, aesthetically-spaced ticks. To force the y-axis to start at a specific value, set explicit ticks instead of (or in addition to) the locator:

import numpy as np
ymin, ymax = 2, df['mag'].max()
plt.gca().set_ylim(ymin, ymax)
plt.gca().set_yticks(np.arange(ymin, np.ceil(ymax) + 1, step))

pick step to match how many ticks you want. set_ylim(bottom=2) alone will clip the axis but MaxNLocator can still choose a first tick below/above 2 rounded to its own "nice" step; only set_yticks with an explicit array guarantees the first tick is exactly 2. If you want auto-chosen intervals but anchored at a fixed start, MaxNLocator doesn't support an anchor point - matplotlib.ticker.IndexLocator(base=step, offset=2) is the locator built for evenly-spaced ticks starting from a fixed offset.

The admin list in utils/variables.py as posted has no commas between entries (just whitespace-separated integers). As literally shown that's a SyntaxError at import time, which would crash the cog on load rather than silently doing nothing - so if the bot does start, this is likely a paste/formatting artifact and your real file has commas. If commas are present and the bug is real: print(admin) running but nothing after the if firing (not even the else branch) points to an unhandled exception inside any(r.id in admin for r in ctx.author.roles). The most common cause is ctx.author not being a fully-populated discord.Member (empty/stale .roles) because the Server Members Intent isn't enabled - check both intents.members = True in code and the toggle in the Discord Developer Portal. Wrap the check in try/except and log the exception to confirm which of these it actually is, rather than guessing further.

"float object is not iterable" in a stateful EMA DoFn almost always means something is trying to iterate over the value read from a ReadModifyWriteStateSpec cell as if it were a collection. ReadModifyWriteStateSpec stores and returns a single value (your running EMA float) via state.read() - you use it directly (current = state.read() or initial_value), you don't loop over it. That iteration pattern (for x in state.read()) is only correct for BagStateSpec, which does return an iterable of buffered elements. Check your DoFn's process() method for a stray for-loop or unpacking (e.g. a, b = state.read()) against the ReadModifyWriteStateSpec cell rather than the BagStateSpec one. Since the exact process() body got cut off, the general fix is: only ever consume each state spec the way its type dictates - scalar read/write for ReadModifyWriteStateSpec, iteration only for BagStateSpec - and make sure on_timer isn't treating the EMA float as a windowed collection when emitting it downstream.
